title: Effort as delight: virya
hookLine: effort is delight in doing good, not strain (Bodhicaryavatara 7)
carry: virya: effort is delight in the good
tomorrow: busy all evening and still lazy? how?

cards: Scroll through workout playlists and the titles shout: grind, no days off, beast mode. Motivational videos pile it on: wake before dawn, outwork everyone.

Effort, in our world, sounds like a clenched jaw and a little guilt. So here's the odd thing. Shantideva opens his chapter on effort, the chapter you'd expect to be all grit, and his definition has no strain in it at all.
He asks, what is effort? And his answer is a word about joy. Not pushing through.
Not discipline. Why would the effort chapter start with delight?

teach.b: Here's his answer, in one line: effort is delight in the good.

The Sanskrit word is virya, and he defines it as eagerness for what's wholesome, kushala. Its opposite, he says, isn't rest. It's laziness, which wears more disguises than you'd expect; that's tomorrow.
So the puzzle solves like this.
For Shantideva, effort is measured by gladness, not by how much it hurts. A kid building a sandcastle as the tide comes in works hard all afternoon and would never call it work.
Or someone cooking for people they love: hours of chopping and stirring, and humming the whole time. That's the shape he's after. Effort powered by dread wears out.
Effort powered by delight comes back the next morning on its own. One honest note, so this doesn't turn into only do what's fun: good things are often hard. Caring for a sick parent is hard.
Learning anything is hard. The delight isn't in the ease; it's in the good itself, in helping, in learning, in getting a little freer.
The task can be heavy. The heart doesn't have to be.

how: In Buddhist teaching, virya (effort, energy) is one of the perfections a bodhisattva cultivates; teachers often present it as gladness in practice and kindness rather than as force.

games.q: what does “delight in the good” mean?
o: effort that comes from gladness about doing good
enjoying good things instead of doing work
a pleasant feeling after you finish hard work

games.q: two kinds of effort — tap the pairs.

s: Shantideva defines effort as forcing yourself through what you hate
he defines it as delight in the good: eagerness for what's wholesome.
for Shantideva, the opposite of effort is rest
the opposite is laziness, and it has disguises; rest comes back later as a strength.
in his view, a hard task can still be done with delight
the delight is in the good itself, not in the task being easy.

games.q: a friend signed up for a charity run and dreads every training morning. what does Shantideva's definition suggest?
o: find what's good in it for her, the cause, the friends, the sunrise, and run for that.
push harder through the dread; the misery is what makes it real effort.
quit training; if it isn't fun every time, it isn't real effort.
games.why: effort, for Shantideva, is delight in the good. the run can stay hard; the gladness is in what it's for.

practice: Choose one small good task within reach: a cup to rinse, a plant to water, a thank-you to start writing. Do it slowly while the sit runs, and look for one thing in it to enjoy: the warm water, the green leaf, the right word.
Let the enjoying count as part of the work.

wordCard.voice: Delight in the good: Shantideva's definition of effort. In Sanskrit, virya, joyful energy for what's wholesome.

orig.note: Sanskrit: energy, effort; for Shantideva, delight in the good.

carryVoice: Your line: virya, effort is delight in the good. A heavy task can have a light heart. Chapter seven, open.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 7.1-7.2 (effort defined as eagerness for the wholesome; its opposites)
